paper_published_in.title: Whole genome comparison of a large collection of mycobacteriophages reveals a continuum of phage genetic diversity
paper_published_in.abstract: The bacteriophage population is large, dynamic, ancient, and genetically diverse. Limited genomic information shows that phage genomes are mosaic, and the genetic architecture of phage populations remains ill-defined. To understand the population structure of phages infecting a single host strain, we isolated, sequenced, and compared 627 phages of Mycobacterium smegmatis. Their genetic diversity is considerable, and there are 28 distinct genomic types (clusters) with related nucleotide sequences. However, amino acid sequence comparisons show pervasive genomic mosaicism, and quantification of inter-cluster and intra-cluster relatedness reveals a continuum of genetic diversity, albeit with uneven representation of different phages. Furthermore, rarefaction analysis shows that the mycobacteriophage population is not closed, and there is a constant influx of genes from other sources. Phage isolation and analysis was performed by a large consortium of academic institutions, illustrating the substantial benefits of a disseminated, structured program involving large numbers of freshman undergraduates in scientific discovery.

results.discovery_notes: The sample was collected in a damp area that had roof covering over it from a school building. It was very moist outside in the air as well as humid from recent rain. The soil was soft in the surrounding area of dirt but, it was tougher under the covering of the building as it was drier. The surrounding area from the soil sample was covered in fallen decaying leaves and roots from larger plants. It was in the foliage area of a plant box where the larger tree type plants with fanning leaves as cover. It was covered by a building ledge so some of the elements would not be able to reach it such as wind, rain, and occasionally moments of sunlight. In the process of one of the labs to create webbed plates that contain plaques through serial dilutions (10^0to 10^-8), it was very interesting to see that our phage sample would only grow plaques in large amounts on the original plate 10^0 instead of the later dilutions of 10^-1 all the way to 10^-8. In our research we noticed that the serial dilutions of our phage sample were very consistent in their growth pattern.  The farthest our sample would create plaques consistently would be to the dilution 10^-3, so our only plates that would show data each time we did a serial dilutions would be 10^0,10^-1,10-^2, and 10^-3; the occasional 10^-4 .  Our phage is finicky and likes not to be tampered with in extra processes such things like enrichment of its environment or intentional changes to its growth patterns.

paper_published_in.title: Whole genome comparison of a large collection of mycobacteriophages reveals a continuum of phage genetic diversity
paper_published_in.abstract: The bacteriophage population is large, dynamic, ancient, and genetically diverse. Limited genomic information shows that phage genomes are mosaic, and the genetic architecture of phage populations remains ill-defined. To understand the population structure of phages infecting a single host strain, we isolated, sequenced, and compared 627 phages of Mycobacterium smegmatis. Their genetic diversity is considerable, and there are 28 distinct genomic types (clusters) with related nucleotide sequences. However, amino acid sequence comparisons show pervasive genomic mosaicism, and quantification of inter-cluster and intra-cluster relatedness reveals a continuum of genetic diversity, albeit with uneven representation of different phages. Furthermore, rarefaction analysis shows that the mycobacteriophage population is not closed, and there is a constant influx of genes from other sources. Phage isolation and analysis was performed by a large consortium of academic institutions, illustrating the substantial benefits of a disseminated, structured program involving large numbers of freshman undergraduates in scientific discovery.

paper_published_in.title: Whole genome comparison of a large collection of mycobacteriophages reveals a continuum of phage genetic diversity
paper_published_in.abstract: The bacteriophage population is large, dynamic, ancient, and genetically diverse. Limited genomic information shows that phage genomes are mosaic, and the genetic architecture of phage populations remains ill-defined. To understand the population structure of phages infecting a single host strain, we isolated, sequenced, and compared 627 phages of Mycobacterium smegmatis. Their genetic diversity is considerable, and there are 28 distinct genomic types (clusters) with related nucleotide sequences. However, amino acid sequence comparisons show pervasive genomic mosaicism, and quantification of inter-cluster and intra-cluster relatedness reveals a continuum of genetic diversity, albeit with uneven representation of different phages. Furthermore, rarefaction analysis shows that the mycobacteriophage population is not closed, and there is a constant influx of genes from other sources. Phage isolation and analysis was performed by a large consortium of academic institutions, illustrating the substantial benefits of a disseminated, structured program involving large numbers of freshman undergraduates in scientific discovery.

paper_published_in.title: Whole genome comparison of a large collection of mycobacteriophages reveals a continuum of phage genetic diversity
paper_published_in.abstract: The bacteriophage population is large, dynamic, ancient, and genetically diverse. Limited genomic information shows that phage genomes are mosaic, and the genetic architecture of phage populations remains ill-defined. To understand the population structure of phages infecting a single host strain, we isolated, sequenced, and compared 627 phages of Mycobacterium smegmatis. Their genetic diversity is considerable, and there are 28 distinct genomic types (clusters) with related nucleotide sequences. However, amino acid sequence comparisons show pervasive genomic mosaicism, and quantification of inter-cluster and intra-cluster relatedness reveals a continuum of genetic diversity, albeit with uneven representation of different phages. Furthermore, rarefaction analysis shows that the mycobacteriophage population is not closed, and there is a constant influx of genes from other sources. Phage isolation and analysis was performed by a large consortium of academic institutions, illustrating the substantial benefits of a disseminated, structured program involving large numbers of freshman undergraduates in scientific discovery.

results.naming_notes: The name of the phage "Agape74" was inspired by the Classical Greek word "agápē", which means the highest form of love, or God's love for humankind.
results.discovery_notes: The environmental sample containing the novel bacteriophage was obtained on 25th August 2014, at 7:48 P.M EDT and 27°C from the GPS Location of 42° 47’ 10’’N and 86°6’6’’W.The sample was collected from very moist soil at 4cm from the ground surface, in an urban setting that is 2m within the proximity of a cement structure. The surrounding environment from where the sample was obtained also included moderate amounts of shrubs and grasses, as well as compost matters. The environmental sample was then isolated and purified using the enrichment method, in which incubation occurred at 32°C over 48 hours.
results.plaque_notes: The following plaque morphology was observed consistently across all 4 phage-titer assays and a final plaque purification: small, uniformly circular plaques of approximately 2 mm in diameter, of very high level of turbidity and with fuzzy edges.
results.lysogeny_notes: The mycobacteriophage Agape74 is a temperate phage and hence could undergo lysogenic cycle to integrate its nucleic acid into the genome of its bacterial host cell. Moreover, Agape74 is also capable of growing at 42°C over an incubation period of 48 hours. However, its growth rate is slower than that at 32°C over the same period of incubation, which is characterized by the lower number of plaques produced at 42°C compared to the number of plaques produced at 32°C.

paper_published_in.title: Whole genome comparison of a large collection of mycobacteriophages reveals a continuum of phage genetic diversity
paper_published_in.abstract: The bacteriophage population is large, dynamic, ancient, and genetically diverse. Limited genomic information shows that phage genomes are mosaic, and the genetic architecture of phage populations remains ill-defined. To understand the population structure of phages infecting a single host strain, we isolated, sequenced, and compared 627 phages of Mycobacterium smegmatis. Their genetic diversity is considerable, and there are 28 distinct genomic types (clusters) with related nucleotide sequences. However, amino acid sequence comparisons show pervasive genomic mosaicism, and quantification of inter-cluster and intra-cluster relatedness reveals a continuum of genetic diversity, albeit with uneven representation of different phages. Furthermore, rarefaction analysis shows that the mycobacteriophage population is not closed, and there is a constant influx of genes from other sources. Phage isolation and analysis was performed by a large consortium of academic institutions, illustrating the substantial benefits of a disseminated, structured program involving large numbers of freshman undergraduates in scientific discovery.

paper_published_in.title: Whole genome comparison of a large collection of mycobacteriophages reveals a continuum of phage genetic diversity
paper_published_in.abstract: The bacteriophage population is large, dynamic, ancient, and genetically diverse. Limited genomic information shows that phage genomes are mosaic, and the genetic architecture of phage populations remains ill-defined. To understand the population structure of phages infecting a single host strain, we isolated, sequenced, and compared 627 phages of Mycobacterium smegmatis. Their genetic diversity is considerable, and there are 28 distinct genomic types (clusters) with related nucleotide sequences. However, amino acid sequence comparisons show pervasive genomic mosaicism, and quantification of inter-cluster and intra-cluster relatedness reveals a continuum of genetic diversity, albeit with uneven representation of different phages. Furthermore, rarefaction analysis shows that the mycobacteriophage population is not closed, and there is a constant influx of genes from other sources. Phage isolation and analysis was performed by a large consortium of academic institutions, illustrating the substantial benefits of a disseminated, structured program involving large numbers of freshman undergraduates in scientific discovery.

Time: 9/1/18 6:31 PM

Location: flower bed near Sutherland West (40.445599..., -79.962766...)

results.plaque_notes: After direct isolation and spot test protocols, Aiya for plaque purification was grown and incubated for 2-5 days on PYCa plate with 1X top agar and G. terrae. Lytic phages generally have clear plaques, whereas lysogenic phages generally have cloudy plaques. Aiya produces clear round plaques with distinct edges that measured ½  mm in diameter.
results.lysogeny_notes: To test for the potential formation of a lysogen, Aiya was plated on PYCa plates with 1X top agar and G. terrae which were then incubated for 5-7 days. If a  mesa, or overgrowth of bacterial cells surrounded by the zone of clearing caused by phage infection and lysis, is present potential lysogens are streaked onto new plate with 1X top agar. Bacterial colonies from this plate are streaked onto experimental (top agar and G. terrae) and control patch assay plates (only base agar). Clearings in the of the experimental plate lawn caused by cell lysis around the patches on the experimental plate would be caused by potential lysogens. Aiya did not create very visible mesas; however, a potential mesa on spot 4 was streaked onto a new plate for a lysogen patch assay. On the experimental plate there were clearings indicative of cell lysis, indicating that Aiya has the potential to undergo lysogeny and form lysogens to infect G. terrae.

paper_published_in.title: Whole genome comparison of a large collection of mycobacteriophages reveals a continuum of phage genetic diversity
paper_published_in.abstract: The bacteriophage population is large, dynamic, ancient, and genetically diverse. Limited genomic information shows that phage genomes are mosaic, and the genetic architecture of phage populations remains ill-defined. To understand the population structure of phages infecting a single host strain, we isolated, sequenced, and compared 627 phages of Mycobacterium smegmatis. Their genetic diversity is considerable, and there are 28 distinct genomic types (clusters) with related nucleotide sequences. However, amino acid sequence comparisons show pervasive genomic mosaicism, and quantification of inter-cluster and intra-cluster relatedness reveals a continuum of genetic diversity, albeit with uneven representation of different phages. Furthermore, rarefaction analysis shows that the mycobacteriophage population is not closed, and there is a constant influx of genes from other sources. Phage isolation and analysis was performed by a large consortium of academic institutions, illustrating the substantial benefits of a disseminated, structured program involving large numbers of freshman undergraduates in scientific discovery.
